D009-D008_h001.question:
It’s been a strange couple of years. About a year and a half ago I had this spell that lasted maybe a month where I felt like I was running on pure engine oil. I barely slept, maybe three hours a night, but I’d get up before dawn feeling wired, not tired. I couldn’t sit still—pacing the house, walking up and down the fields for no reason, hands always moving. My wife said I was talking so fast she couldn’t keep up, jumping from fixing the tractor to planting a new crop to plans for buying more land. My mood would flip on a dime: one minute joking and laughing, the next snapping at her and the kids over nothing. I didn’t think anything was wrong, but they were scared; my brother actually brought me into the hospital because they thought I might hurt myself or someone by the way I was acting.

Since then, for the past year, it’s been the opposite. I wake up heavy, sad every day, like there’s no point. Things I used to enjoy—working the soil, Sunday dinners—feel empty. Just thinking about simple tasks wears me out. I’ve caught myself thinking it’d be easier if I just didn’t wake up, though I haven’t made any plans. It’s gotten hard to keep the farm going.
D009-D008_h001.options:
A. Anorexia Nervosa
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D009-D008_h002.question:
It’s been a really hard year. I used to be so proud of being a good teacher, raising two kids, helping students succeed, but now I feel empty about all of it, like none of it matters. Most days I just sit in the living room, staring at the TV without really watching. I’m exhausted all the time, even just getting dressed feels like climbing a mountain. I keep thinking my family would be better off without me. I’ve caught myself thinking, “I should just end it,” over and over, though I haven’t made a plan. It got so bad that my husband brought me to the hospital because he was scared I might hurt myself.

What’s confusing is that a bit over a year ago, before this long low spell, I had about a month where I felt “too good.” I barely slept for nights on end and didn’t feel tired at all. I was talking nonstop, pacing around the house, starting big projects—reorganizing the whole attic, planning a community tutoring program—jumping from one thing to another. One minute I’d be laughing, the next snapping at my husband for no real reason. I knew it was unusual, but I didn’t think I was sick then.
D009-D008_h002.options:
A. Anorexia Nervosa
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D009-D008_h003.question:
I’ve had these “high” periods on and off, but the one last spring really scared my husband. For about a month, I was on top of the world. I felt amazing, like I’d finally figured everything out. I only slept maybe three hours a night, but I’d wake up buzzing, full of ideas for the branch, texting staff at all hours, calling old friends I hadn’t seen in years. At work I couldn’t stop talking in meetings, jumping from one plan to another. I was going out constantly, organizing dinners, networking events, barely home. My regional manager actually called HR because I was so over the top and wouldn’t slow down; they suggested I see someone, and my husband was talking about taking me to the hospital because he was worried I might do something reckless, like start approving loans on impulse.

Then things crashed. For the past year I’ve mostly felt the opposite—always on the verge of tears, crying in my office or in the bathroom. I can’t get myself to start even simple tasks; my energy is gone. Just getting out of bed to go to the bank feels impossible. I’ve fallen behind on reports, needed my assistant to cover for me. I keep thinking it would be easier if I just didn’t wake up, though I don’t have a plan to hurt myself.
D009-D008_h003.options:
A. Anorexia Nervosa
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D009-D008_h004.question:
It’s been a really up‑and‑down year. The low part has been going on for about a year straight. I come home from the archives and just sit in the dark. I’ve stopped seeing friends, stopped answering messages. It’s like everything inside went flat; I don’t really feel sad, just blank, like someone muted all my emotions. Even thinking through a simple cataloguing problem exhausts me. My mind gets tired in minutes, and I make stupid mistakes at work.

Sometimes, walking over the river bridge to the library, I get this sudden urge to just climb over and let go, or when a bus comes I feel this pull to step in front of it. It’s not that I make plans, but the impulse is strong enough that I’ve had to grip the railings. That scared me enough that my supervisor called an ambulance once and I ended up in the hospital for a few days.

Before this, about a year and a half ago, I had a month where I felt amazing. I barely slept—maybe two, three hours—and didn’t feel tired. I couldn’t sit still, was constantly pacing or rearranging shelves at work. I talked nonstop; my coworkers had trouble getting a word in. I was suddenly obsessed with sex, messaging multiple people, watching porn all night. I knew I was different, but it didn’t really mess up my job like this low phase has.
D009-D008_h004.options:
A. Anorexia Nervosa
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D009-D008_h005.question:
It’s been a rough year. For most of the last twelve months, I’ve felt like I’m running on empty. I drag myself to the plant, but I just stand there staring at the machines or my clipboard. Jobs that used to be automatic now feel impossible to start. I get tired just thinking about a shift, like all the strength’s drained out of me. I’ve had days where I just sit in my car in the parking lot and cry for no clear reason, trying to pull myself together before going in. My wife keeps asking what’s wrong because I tear up over the smallest thing.

It got so bad a few months ago that I started thinking everyone would be better off without me. I actually saved up my pain pills and one night I took a bunch of them, planning not to wake up. My wife found me and I ended up in the hospital for that.

What’s confusing is that about a year and a half ago I had almost the opposite spell that lasted about a month. I barely slept—maybe three hours a night—but I’d wake up wired, pacing the house before work and then racing around the factory. I was talking nonstop in meetings, jumping from one idea to another, couldn’t stand any silence. I was short-tempered too; the guys would ask a simple question and I’d snap at them, feel like everyone was too slow.

At home I was constantly after my wife for sex, like my drive was stuck on high. I felt charged up all the time, but I still mostly kept things together at work—just more on edge and intense than usual. Then it just sort of burned out, and over time I slipped into this long, low stretch I can’t seem to climb out of.
D009-D008_h005.options:
A. Anorexia Nervosa
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D009-D008_h006.question:
It’s kind of swung back and forth this year.  

About six months ago I hit this “high” that lasted a good two months. I was on the road nonstop and felt like I didn’t need rest. I couldn’t sit still at truck stops – pacing, cleaning the cab at 2 a.m., starting side projects I’d never finish. One minute I’d be joking and feeling on top of the world, and the next I’d snap at dispatch or other drivers over nothing. I was calling old friends, chatting up strangers at diners, going out with people I’d just met instead of sleeping. I even hooked up a few times with women I barely knew, no protection, in places I normally would never risk it. Somehow I still managed to keep working through that stretch.  

Then it crashed into this really empty spell that’s been on and off for about two months now. I sleep 8–9 hours and wake up feeling like I haven’t slept at all. The cab feels hollow, like I’m just a body driving. I’ve missed runs, screwed up schedules, and my boss warned me I might lose my job. I’ve had a couple times where it got dark enough I scared myself, and my ex actually brought me into the ER because she was worried I might hurt myself.
D009-D008_h006.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D009-D008_h007.question:
I’ve been working nights at the warehouse as a security guard, and about four months ago something really flipped in me. For almost two months I was constantly on edge and snapping at people over nothing—coworkers, my wife, even drivers just pulling up to the gate. I couldn’t sit still in the booth; I’d pace the lot, check doors over and over, start extra patrols they never asked for. I took on every overtime shift, tried to reorganize the whole security schedule on my own, like I had to fix everything right away.

I also started driving way too fast between sites, weaving through traffic like I was invincible. My wife said I was scaring her and the grandkids. It got so bad one night that my supervisor called my wife and told her to take me to the ER because he was worried I’d hurt myself or someone else.

Then it all crashed. For the past two months I’ve been crying for no clear reason, especially at night. I fall asleep, then wake up at 2 or 3 a.m. and just lie there, staring at the ceiling, unable to get back to sleep. I’ve been calling in sick because I can’t function at work. My wife says I’m not myself at all.
D009-D008_h007.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D009-D008_h008.question:
It kinda comes in these swings. A few months ago I went through this stretch, maybe two months, where I just felt constantly on edge and wired. Little things at work would set me off—an email phrased the wrong way and I’d snap at people or stew for hours. At the same time, I had this crazy amount of energy. I’d be pacing around the warehouse, rearranging routes, volunteering for extra shifts, starting new projects before finishing old ones. I barely sat down. I was driving way too fast between sites, cutting people off, and there were a couple nights I went out, did a lot more coke than I usually would, without really caring what might happen.

Then it crashed. The last two months have been the opposite. I cry at stupid things—commercials, a comment from my boss. Sometimes I’m in the bathroom at work just trying to stop tearing up. Sleep is a mess because of these awful, vivid nightmares almost every night; I wake up sweating and exhausted. I’ve missed days of work, fallen behind on scheduling, and my manager’s warned me my performance isn’t acceptable. It’s gotten bad enough I’m honestly scared I’m going to lose my job or do something that gets me hurt.
D009-D008_h008.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D009-D008_h009.question:
It’s kind of split into two totally different versions of me.

When I’m “up,” it starts like this really wired, pissed‑off energy. Little things set me off—someone tweaking a frame in my cut, an email taking too long—and I snap or get sarcastic and mean. I can’t sit still in the edit bay; I’m pacing, clicking around on three timelines at once, bouncing from project to project. I sleep maybe a few hours, but I don’t even feel tired. My sex drive goes through the roof—I’m on dating apps nonstop, sexting, hooking up with people I barely know. I also blow through money: cameras, lenses, random gear I don’t need, expensive dinners. I ran up my credit cards over those two months, but I was still showing up to work and even getting praise for how “driven” I seemed.

Then I crash. For the last two months I’ve felt like someone turned the lights off inside. I’m just…low all the time. Getting started on a cut feels impossible. I lie in bed staring at the ceiling for hours before I can fall asleep, even though I’m exhausted. I started missing deadlines, calling in sick, barely eating. Eventually my boss insisted I take leave because I wasn’t functioning, and my mom brought me to the ER because she got scared I might hurt myself.
D009-D008_h009.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D009-D008_h010.question:
It’s like my mood’s been on a rollercoaster the last few months. About four months ago I had this stretch, maybe two months, where I felt incredible. I barely needed sleep, maybe three or four hours, and I’d still get up buzzing with energy. On the subway I was volunteering for every extra shift, rearranging schedules, suggesting new routes and safety procedures like I was running the whole system. At home I started planning two side businesses at once, and I even put a big chunk of our savings into some online “transport investment” scheme without really checking what it was. My wife was furious. I’d go from laughing and cracking jokes to snapping at her and the kids within minutes.

Then it’s like the bottom fell out. For the last two months I’ve felt hollow, like there’s just nothing inside. I wake up at 3 or 4 a.m. every day and just stare at the ceiling. I’ve been calling in sick because I can’t face the tunnel or the passengers. My supervisor told me to take leave because I was making mistakes, and my wife was so worried about how flat and empty I’d become that she brought me to the emergency room. They even talked about admitting me because they were concerned I might not be safe.
D009-D008_h010.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D009-D008_h011.question:
It’s been a rough year. For about nine months now I’ve been stuck in this really low place. I tear up over nothing—commercials, a customer raising their voice—and once I start, I can’t pull it together. My head feels exhausted all the time; even trying to work out a finance deal or focus on inventory drains me in minutes. I used to be sharp with numbers, now I just stare at the screen. I’ve been missing days at the dealership and my sales have tanked.  

Sleep is awful. I keep having these intense, disturbing dreams—sometimes about crashing cars, sometimes about my ex taking my kid away—and I wake up sweating and scared, then can’t get back to sleep.  

Before this, around last spring, I had this three‑week stretch where I was the opposite. I was wired, full of energy, pacing the showroom, snapping at coworkers and customers over small things. I felt unbeatable, like I could sell anything to anyone, and I was constantly calling people, networking, going out. It didn’t really mess up my life then; I still showed up and functioned. But this long low period now… it’s really knocked my life off track.

A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia

D009-D008_h012.question:
For most of the last year, it’s like I’ve had two completely different settings.

The long stretch has been this dull, dragged-out low. For about nine months now I’ve felt like someone unplugged me. I’m exhausted pretty much all the time, even on days I don’t have many clients and sleep in. It’s weird because I don’t even really feel sad; it’s more like I can’t feel much of anything at all, like I’m watching my own life from the outside. I wake up multiple times a night and then just stare at the ceiling for an hour, so my sleep is all broken. I’ve cut back my classes, clients have dropped off, and I’ve had to call in sick a lot because I just can’t get through the day.

Then there are these “up” times, like the one about three weeks long a couple months ago, where I flip. I get really on edge and snap at clients over small stuff. I can’t sit still—constantly pacing between sets, planning new programs, trying to launch three new bootcamps at once. I start thinking I’m destined to be some revolutionary fitness guru, like I’ve got this special calling. Last time, I got so amped and aggressive they took me to the ER and kept me overnight because they were worried I might lose control and hurt someone at the gym.
D009-D008_h012.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia

D009-D008_h013.question:
I’m here because things have swung so far up and down that it’s started to feel dangerous.

About a year ago I crashed into this long, heavy period. For the last nine months I’ve been exhausted all the time. Getting out of bed to even open my laptop feels like climbing a mountain. I wake up around 3 or 4 a.m. almost every night and just stare at the ceiling, and then spend the day dragging myself around the apartment. I cry at random things—emails from my supervisor, a commercial, nothing at all. I’ve fallen behind on my thesis, stopped meeting friends, stopped cooking. My advisor has suggested I take a leave because I’m not functioning.

But before this, I had this stretch—maybe three weeks—where I was “on fire.” I was snapping at people over tiny things, but also staying up late, outlining new chapters, starting side projects, convinced I’d rewrite the whole field. I felt weirdly invincible, like there was no way I could fail. It got so intense that my friends and my advisor actually pushed me to go to the hospital because they were worried I might do something reckless or hurt myself, even though I didn’t feel sick at the time.

A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia

D009-D008_h014.question:
It’s been a rough year. For about nine months now I’ve been dragging myself through each day. I get choked up over nothing—interviewing a victim’s family, watching a news clip—and I’ll have to step away so the guys at the precinct don’t see me tearing up. My head feels like it’s wading through mud; even writing reports or following a lead feels exhausting after just a few minutes. At home, I’m too wiped to really talk to my wife. Nights are the worst: I keep having these graphic nightmares about crime scenes and shootings, over and over, and I wake up sweating and can’t get back to sleep. It’s gotten bad enough that my performance has slipped, and my supervisor’s pulled me aside about it.

But a few months back, before this long slump, I had about three weeks where I felt unstoppable. I barely sat still—constantly pacing, starting new investigations, volunteering for extra shifts, reworking old cases. My mood would flip fast: one minute I was on top of the world, the next I’d snap at colleagues. I became convinced I was meant to single‑handedly clean up the city, like I had some special calling other detectives didn’t. My wife was worried I’d get myself or someone else hurt the way I was charging into situations.

A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia

D009-D008_h015.question:
It kind of comes in waves. About a year ago I had this stretch, maybe three weeks, where I felt amazing. I was up before dawn, cleaning all the rooms, taking extra shifts, even offering to reorganize closets that weren’t mine to touch. I wasn’t tired at all. I’d walk fast all day, talk to everyone, like I had this endless battery. I kept thinking, “I can do anything now, maybe start my own cleaning business, hire people, make a fortune.” That’s not like me. I usually doubt myself. But then I was so sure nothing could go wrong, I didn’t even listen when my boss told me to slow down.

Then it all crashed. For the last nine months, I’ve been mostly the opposite. I cry at the smallest thing—commercials, a broken glass. Just getting out of bed to go clean a single room feels impossible. I’m exhausted all the time. I wake up two, three times a night and just lie there. I’ve missed work, they cut my hours, and my sister had to stay with me for a while because I just couldn’t manage the house or even feeding myself properly.

D009-D008_h016.question:

I wake up feeling like there’s a weight on my chest, and nothing feels enjoyable anymore—not my students, not playing Chopin, nothing. I keep replaying tiny mistakes in my head, like snapping at a student or canceling a lesson, and I feel like I’m this horrible, selfish person who deserves to suffer for it.

My mind feels thick, like I’m thinking through mud. Planning a simple lesson or even following a score feels confusing. My sister found me and took me to the hospital; I was admitted for a few days.

I barely slept, was overflowing with energy, rearranging my entire curriculum, starting new projects, talking nonstop. I’d get distracted by every little noise in the studio, but I felt fantastic and just kept going.     D. Bipolar I Disorder

D009-D008_h017.question:

I keep blaming myself for little things, like if a household bill is a day late, I feel like I’m a terrible person.
